review:
The game was initially released with files missing, which has since been fixed. What you have now is a wonderful RPG where you get to play as a mighty dragon. I played this game quite a bit over the years and was very surprised to see it pop up on steam.

The I of the dragon is quite relentless in its default difficulty (5) but can be adjusted to either 1 or 10. I do not recommend putting it higher as the game was clearly not properly designed for it. The game is rather slow paced by default and turning all enemies into tanks that just take way too long to kill is not fun, only tedious.

There's 3 different Dragon classes; Necromancer, Mage and Warrior, the latter focussing on its fire breath over magic use. Each class has unique skills and specializes in different stats (which are cheaper to level up). The necromancer ends up being the middle ground class with some summoning options.

As you level up you can spend points on stats and purchase spells (for said points). Its up to the player to balance it out.

Spells in this game are quite awesome and deserve to be mentioned seperatly. There is a wide range of spells and with the ability to litterally summon mountains and giant craters you can terraform the land around you quite dramatically impacting enemy movement as well. Yes after some time the land will turn back to its original state but it takes quite a while and it looks impressive. Really makes the player feel powerful.

However, as for downsides; There are a couple of segments in the game where you are forced to play as other characters and these segments are just plain terrible. There's no way around it, they should never have made it in the game. However they happen relatively late and can be finished somewhat quick with some practice.

Overall,  if you like the idea of controlling a mighty dragon that grows incredibly strong over time, get this game. Yes it's a bit dated but the game is unique enough that there really isn't a better modern alternative. This IS the best dragon RPG out there.

[b]Once Upon a Time, when the gaming community was young, and coptures - old, game developers had the guts to try and put some new and truly unique stuff into their games, rather then just copy - paste a single successful formula for every given genre. Giving this game a try, you will learn why, and come to appreciate the fact these good old times have past. [/b]

This game used to amaze back in the day, it was the first time gamers were given a try to play an RPG that doesn't blindly follow the "knight in shiny armour killing the archdemon" cliche. The graphics rocked (in 2002), the feeling of flight on your own set of wings, and the ability to dive down and catch your rival to have a bloody snack up in the air were amusing. BUT back in the day we were used to having to relearn and remaster the controls for every new game that we played, we were used to having to deal with clunky controls and some minor inconveniences in the overall gameplay. The tradition of implementing high quality, touching stories with complex characters had not yet been settled in the industry. We loved games mainly for their gameplay and the fresh experiences they brought us.
Today most games deliver several genres in one pack, like shooters where you can fly a plane or ride a car e.t.c. The things that made this game look cool more than a decade ago are fairly trivial for the modern gamer, while the flaws look outrageous. The game has an unappealing story, the quests are boring and repetitive (go to an area kill all the monster, then go to another locations and do "the exact same thing over and over again"), the controls are oldschool (clunky + underworked = inconvenient). This game is bad by all modern game standards, but this game was developed in the times when those standards were only a work in progress.

[b] Summary: [/b] If you are a player from back in the day, taking the low price of the game to notice, you might want to take a glance to the past with this one, it might be a useful experience. Or if you are new to gaming and want to feel how it realy was to play them "good old games" you might want to get it while on sale. In other cases take a second thought before you press the "buy" button.

Full Disclosure: Re-released game, bought original and bought Steam version during $2 sale. Big fan of GOG.com.
I bought this game back in 2004 and played it then. It was alright, especially since games that let you play as a dragon are few and far between. Yeah, it got fairly repetitive since the majority of the game is hunting down monster spawners and killing then, usually via fly-by attacks. (Would've been better if they used mouse-based flight a-la Freelancer since you use said mouse for some controls. And yes, Freelancer came out before this.)
However, this is no longer that game, and even at $2, I can't recommend it. The controls are still awkward, but now they're worse since you can't remap the keys unless you use a fan-made patch. Also, the game has a CTD problem trying to play the opening movie unless you delete it, and trying to rotate the camera is especially painful as sometimes it starts moving right away, and sometimes it takes up to a full second before it even starts moving. If this was turn-based, it'd only be annoying, but this game is very much action-based. (This is also fixed with a fan-made patch.)
The devs have already gone on record saying that there won't be any patches or improvements to the game as they have lost the source code. Look guys, if you don't have the source code and/or can't fix any problems that arise with the game, DON'T RELEASE THE GAME. The gameplay has gone from "not bad" to "broken mess" simply because these issues can't be fixed due to being unable to update the game for modern systems. The saddest thing is, GOG.com has set a standard for updating old games, and this falls well below it.
Fix the controls so somebody doesn't need three hands to play the game/restore the ability to remap keys, fix the CTD issues, and the lag when trying to rotate the camera, and this game might be worth the asking price. As it is, this game is a broken mess and despite the graphics not aging well, it might be worth playing again.
EDIT: BTW, those review scores up there at the top of the page from Actiontrip and Gameshark? Those are from the '04 edition. The Gameshark site isn't even around anymore.

Is this a good game?

Not by modern standards, no.

However, it does have several things going for it.

1. You get to play as an actual dragon. Not a dragon rider or a dragon in human form or another cop-out, a big, scaly, winged, reptilian dragon who flies around using magic and fire, frost, or poison to destroy evil (and abducting people and animals when hungry).

2. The gameplay loop is repetitive, but if you can overlook the clunkiness it's fairly satisfying. In particular, levelling up is rare enough to be rewarding yet also frequent enough to be a constant motivator throughout the game. It doesn't make the mistake many other games make where you level up 10 times in the first minute and then near the end it takes over an hour to level up once, which also means that you keep growing stronger steadily throughout the game.

3. The graphics are horribly outdated, but the developers clearly did, in my opinion, the best they could with the limited technology available at the time (which, for the record, is over 20 years ago). If you're a fan of traditional RPGs you'll probably appreciate the work done here.

And last, but certainly not least, and in fact possibly the most important part:

4. It's an actual game. Even with all the flaws it's clear to me that this is a product from before greed overtook the gaming industry. Developers sat down for this game and asked themselves what people might enjoy. Not what would get them addicted, not what would keep them coming back to spend more money, but what would actually be fun and entertaining.

Even the 4 quests where you have to play a human (which are all terrible) were clearly put in there because the developers thought they were important to the story or they would add some variation in between being a dragon. The latter of which is thoughtful but unnecessary.
_____
So overall I recommend this game not necessarily because it's good. Its age is showing with outdated graphics, clunky gameplay, a story so straightforward as to almost be bland, and a camera which is constantly trying to get you killed.

I recommend this game because it's from an era where games were meant to be fun. Even if it's only for 20 hours, because it's not a very big game. It starts out with an interesting idea ("What if you're a literal dragon going around slaying monsters and destroying lairs while protecting people") and then tries to make that idea work (flight, an abundance of spells to augment your natural weapons, a straightforward levelling system which lets you specialise your character).

Overall, my recommendation is as much a criticism of the modern gaming industry as it is an endorsement of this specific game, but I would certainly encourage people to buy it (or at least wishlist it for a sale). I'd go so far as to say that a modern version which focuses on addressing issues born from technological limitations of 20 years past would possibly serve as an even better contrast against modern greed-based designs.

This is a game that deserves a reboot or a remaster because it didn't age well. Conceptually and mechanically this game stands out as something amazing, but bugs and control issues just ruin the experience. In the end, I absolutely love this game, but i don't want to actually play this game. 

The I of the Dragon is a weird genre and I think "RPG" is selling it short. Instead, it reminds me more of an Actraiser or Herzog Zwei where you have one powerful avatar to support an RTS.

The core gameplay involves diablo-esque style where you click around to explore territories fighting monsters and monster-spawning lairs. You have your basic breath weapon, you can grab small things to eat them, and have a growing list of spells. As you get XP you raise your stats and learn new skills. Your dragon quickly grows into a force of nature.

But those monster lairs will respawn endlessly in the wilds and no dragon can tame the lands. The only way to stop them permanently is to build a human city. Once a city is built, lairs stop respawning and monsters will stay dead. But even then you aren't entirely safe. Monsters can still invade from outside territories and you'll need to strengthen the towns to defend against it or personally fly back to their aid. 

The exact combination of mechanics makes you feel like a powerful guardian to these tiny humans. It isn't particularly deep but it stands out. Mentally you're trying to balance advancing your personal quests with protecting the various towns you've built.

And then comes the bad... The controls make me feel like I'm wrestling with the dragon instead of controlling it. I've tried remapping keys, I've tried getting the hang of it, and the best solution I've had is excessive pause abuse to make sure my actions queued properly.  

There are two control schemes that are both active at all times, the mouse can click to move and the keyboard gives you direct control. Using the mouse makes it near impossible to precisely dodge incoming fire but touching the keyboard activates auto-targeting which also causes my dragon to turn to face to wrong unit. Neither scheme well on it's own but together they are broken to a whole new level.

This isn't even mentioning that the keyboard uses all four corners: The numberpad, the arrows, The control and Z keys, and the F12 key. It's like they wanted to spread out your controls to to require four hands and only some of it is remappable in the options. 

The general awkwardness of controls is made even worse by imprecise pathfinding and AI and flat out bugs. I'll often use the "Eat monster" command in a desperate attempt to heal but it just won't activate... or it will and my dragon will decide to just circle around the target unable to find an angle of attack... or worse it'll ignore that it was an "Eat" action and just breath fire becoming a stationary target for the enemies. Oooor.... the turbospin when your mouse cursor reaches the side of the screen and is tied to a modern machine's frame rate! AAAAAAAAAAHHHHHHHHH
 
I'm willing to overlook alot, write off managable jank or acknowledge outdated design choices but the flaws here are too prominent to shrug it off. It's just not fun.

As I said, conceptually and mechanically this game is great. I played the heck out of the non-steam version it in college and enjoyed it immensely. 

But without a remaster that fixes the issues, I can't recommend this. No matter how cool the concept, no matter epic this is, I can't see an audience that I'd actually see recommend the game to outside "Look at this concept". Sigh, please someone reboot this.

Yet another oldie masterpiece that I grew up with! And on Steam!
I was very happy upon stumbling into it because I thought the game disappeared.. Still got the physical copy, but getting it in its original and English language in its vanilla version was quite the experience.

As the name itself tells, although being a bit confusing as the [i]I[/i] stands for [i]Eye,[/i] one of the reasons why I had no luck finding it, and you play as a dragon.
Yeah!
This is one of the few videogames where you actually control your dragon!
No, no spells to transform into a dragon or control a summoned dragon by yourself as a magician in some RPG videogame.. But pure dragon without anything attached to it!

The game's got very simple controls, which is unfortunately the downside of it aswell, as there's not much to this game besides conquering the areas from monsters as the game's descriptions do explain to the detail on their own.
Feeding the dragon, managing the statistics, including learning various spells, and its breath capacity. There's no option to land somewhere, you're gonna be flying the entire time, forward, altering the direction of the flight, and shifting the height of the flight.. That's pretty much all that's there to it for the controls.

Still, there's something satisfying in playing as a dragon and using spells..
That sure dragged me into the game and the time truly flew by without me realizing so. Yes, the playtime of mine does reflect the length of the entire story.. So it's not like this game is that short for what it's got to offer.

When it comes to the variety of dragons, there are three of them.. Which is already covered albeit vaguely in the descriptions.


Now, why I'd recommend this game..
- The main reason, obviously, because it's one of the few videogames out there where you play as a dragon. Without any limitations to it. It's not like the expectations to see dragons who could do various tricks as we see in some movies is to be seen in the game, as the game's very old by today.. Still, it's achieved a lot for what has been available at that time.
- Another reason is the soundtrack. Yup, the soundtrack is amazing. Fits just perfectly to the theme of the game.
- The length of the game is amazing! Far from a shortie, especially if you decide to clear each area to the brim just like me.. And I have yet to finish the game.
I should be at about.. 70% of completion after almost twenty hours.

I guess, that's it..
I can't deny being blinded by the nostalgia, but no matter how hard I tried, I couldn't have found a better videogame where you play as a pure dragon.. This is the best and only one I have found so far.. And I searched for years, for hours on a daily basis for it. No luck, but this hidden gem did the trick.

Have fun!

In a short summery, I of the Dragon is one of those games that has a concept that is for some unknown reason, Extremely difficult to grasp, even today. A game where you play as a fully fledged, Fully flying fire breathing Dragon. Does it succeed where other games failed? Kind of.

Playing as a dragon is one of those things that doesn't seem to have a Major market in. Besides games like Spyro, Dragon games have been in the Meh to Insulting. I of the Dragon has been on my radar for this exact reason. There have been too few games that let you take a look through the looking glass and let you Play as a dragon rather than Slay the dragon. I of the Dragon can satisfy that thirst for Dragon Content, but its far from perfect.

The game is from the early 2000's, so unless you grew up in that era or don't care about graphics, you might not like this. This is from an age where games tried to experiment a lot, and this was definitely an experiment. It feels like some mish mash of a Strategy game, but you directly play as the faction hero of the army. I kind of like this feeling. Personally I'd like a game thats basically a dragon life simulator, but this has a lot of moving parts in it. The game has a Lot of spells and territories for you to play with, yet so far I sense a pattern in the game. Build town, Destroy Lairs, Kill Monsters, Repeat. It wouldn't be that bad but the controls for this game are kind of a nightmare.

The controls are Dated as hell, coming from an era before WASD became the standard keyboard mapping, so I regularly find myself having to switch between the arrow keys and the mouse. It can be extremely aggravating to aim at one of the flying enemies of the game and having them miss your fire ball, or having your breath attack not do as much as you want. The fire ball being tedious with flying enemies because some of them Never stay still. And you have to do it. you have to Kill Every Single Monster on the map. Which means you'll have to track down every single monster and kill them. Total Monster Genocide. 

With all that said though, I still had fun. I enjoy the old school presentation of the game, though the voice acting could be better. Some Models in the game are a bit off though. The Dragons themselves look amazing, but some of the models for the NPCs you talk to in the game either don't have enough detail or have an uncanny valley of early 2000's jank. 

Despite its issues I find the game has a lot of charm. And like many games of the time, the creature designs are strange and alien. Like a Lovecraftian nightmare, in a good way. If you like games where you play as a Dragon, this is one of the earliest examples, and one of the best on PC.

The first half of [b]2000s[/b] was pretty much the last time we had games that both looked competitive and offered us some fresh and unique gameplay. While having things like another [b]Assassin's Creed[/b] game, another [b]Call of Duty[/b] game and so on on regular basis nowadays, it's hard to imagine that there were times when we used to have stuff like [b]Sacrifice[/b], [b]Messiah[/b], [b]Evolva[/b] and [b]Giants: Citizen Kabuto[/b] (if you're about to go to [b]GOG[/b] to buy those after reading this, then you're a) awesome and b) old).

[b]The I of the Dragon[/b] is another one of such games from that exact time period. Surprisingly, this one came from Russia. “Surprisingly” because it looks pretty competitive (even today it looks more than fine and have all chances to be enjoyed by the new generation of players) and doesn't feel nearly as frustrating as [b]Sea Dogs[/b] (which is a bugged hell even today, after it was released in [b]Steam[/b] not so long ago).

Sure, [b]The I of the Dragon[/b] can be pretty rough. The camera is a complete disaster, about half of the time your goals are [i]terribly[/i] explained, while some parts of the game are really, [i]really[/i] poorly balanced. Especially those, in which they take away your strong leveled up character, give you a unit that dies from a single shot and make you walk through the map full of strong enemies that spawn with no end. [i]Man[/i], those parts suck ass... But all in all? It's one of those fresh and awesome games from early [b]2000[/b]s that you should probably try at least once.

Long story short, we have a mix between good ol' [b]Magic Carpet[/b] and some sort of tower defense. By controlling “powerful” dragon (who dies a lot because you didn't praise the sun hard enough), we'll build towns (one town per map, so, make sure to protect and upgrade what you have), level up, destroy enemy lairs and, well, fight stuff. Some main quests are included to make your life harder. No secondary goals, though. Which sucks, since this game is heavily open-world-like (you'll need to travel from map to map, but the time will keep going on all maps and the enemies will try to attack your cities at all maps at the same exact time) and having more things to do will be pretty fun.

But it's not like the game feels lacking, or something. Quite the opposite, the main quests will give you enough challenge, while the main gameplay is addictive enough to give you enough motivation to keep going. I mean, seriously. Even though most of the time it's something like “build the town, protect the city, upgrade the town as much as you can, destroy all enemy lairs, collect the rewards, level up your dragon, kill all monsters, move to another map”, you won't feel bad about doing it again and again. Just because it's fun and there are enough different ways to achieve your goals.

There are also some juicy small details that make this game even more awesome. Like, you'll be able to eat small enemies. Heck, you'll actually [i]need[/i] to do that. Because hunger. And if there are no enemies around? You can eat some guys from your own town. Because screw dem peasants (ah, [b]Sir Chauncey[/b]! [i]How are[/i] you feeling today?). You can also switch between the first and third person views, you can learn different spells, etc, etc, etc.

In other words, there'll be exploration, there'll be action, there'll be some [b]RTS[/b]-like elements, but all in all, even though this game takes heck of a lot from [b]Magic Carpet[/b] (there's even a funny little nod to [b]BULLFROG[/b]'s masterpiece), it's hard to fully compare it with anything. [b]The I of the Dragon[/b] is [b]The I of the Dragon[/b] and if you're tired of playing the same exact game again and again nowadays, you should totally look back and try it. It's totally worth it, even though you'll need to suffer through some rough edges here and there.

Many people said here about bugs, controls, problems, etc. Earlier I had original CD and what I can say, that there always were some problems with it; as I've heard, earlier developers have lost workdata of this game and couldn't fix many things by then. There were some fan-fixes, but still they've couldn't fix all. In many cases game haven't worked at all. There were no background music, chashes on a map change, control freezes. Now I see that the Steam team and community is really working on it, trying to make things better. And they really doing things better — the issue with background music (wich simply haven't worked on a platforms higher than Win2000) now is solved and gone. For now they've really solved many old issues. All works fine. Earlier I've played and passed all it through on Windows 2000 (for the original version of the game it looks like the only OS with wich The I of The Dragon works without any problems at all), Windows XP (haven't worked at all without serious manipulations, at least in my case neither I, nor my friends couldn't fix it and launch — it was completely broken), Windows 7 (worked fine but without music, hehe; sometimes had a control freezes). This version I've tired on Windows 8; I haven't play it long for now, mostly for testing, though, but by this time I haven't found any really serious issues, if not count one with startup-video that plays souns but has black screen instead the video. But with comparison with all other what was with it earlier... it's a complete minor.

And by that time were lack of guides about how you can fix all these problems; earlier at some problems were no answers at all; now It was surprisingly to find there many of them here, on steam + support. I think, with some time and one day they'll fix last serious issues with it.

For now, you will probably need to deal with having some technical issues, but known bug fixes now you can find in the community guides. Earlier, many years ago, there was NONE of that.

About controls; some said that you will need all of the keyboard + complete mouse, but it is a little not fair. Controls really can be a little bit complicated before you get used to them, because you'll need many keys for MAGIC (numbers, and, if I remember correctly, F-s), but basically what you'll really need for comfortable game — arrows on keyboard, maybe WASD, tab, left shift and space + one or two keys for aim. And a map. And that's all. More or less controls of an old standart for two hands; you'll need mouse only to change angle of a view (or set this separately on keyboard) or aim on enemy on wich dragon doesn't aim automatically by some reasons (usually landscape's specs). You can change all the keys (now it is working, at least on Win8x64 — earlier it worked only on Win2000, at least for me), and with some experiments find the comfortable control settings of your own.
Back in the original version there already were normal controls set. Now you'll maybe need to find a fine settings by your own by playing with them for some time, but that's not such an awful thing.

This is quite possibly one of my favorite games I've played in a LONG time. I never even knew this game existed till I stumbled upon it on the store for 90% off ($0.93 CAN.) Frankly any game out there that lets me play as a mother f***ing Dragon is usually always an instant purchase, as games like that are far and few between, and sadly most of them are not that good either. This one happens to be a mixed bag. This game does suffer from problems, and I will explain.

This game is old, 2004. There hasn't been any work on updating this by the Devs, as according to the forums, the Devs don't have the source files. Thankfully though some loyal fans have made some patches to fix problems, like the music not playing, the intro movie not playing, not being able to change controls, slightly improving the graphics, etc. I've played both the normal and patched versions. I never experienced any crashes as stated by other people.

My main gripe with it was the controls. This was the main reason why I never actually finished the game. I got tired trying to fight with the controls. The fan patch does help improve them, but I still found myself fighting with them when fighting harder enemies in the later stages of the game.

In terms of the gameplay, you are a dragon. You fly around, using your attacks and spells to kill monsters and spawners, gain XP to level up to upgrade your stats and learn new attacks/spells, collect gems to gain more power to learn more spells, grab enemies and devour them, and f*** s*** up! There really isn't much for variety in anything though. You go to an area, kill everything, move onto the next, repeat. Some people may not like that at all.

You have a selection of 3 types of dragons. Fire, Ice, and Acid. Each one has different starting stats, and a variety of different kinds of attacks/spells. Everything from Fireball, Ice storm, to summoning zombie minions, and even opening a giant fissure in the ground to kill your enemies! Each Dragon class also plays slightly differently as well. The Fire Dragon being the big Tank/Damage dealer, getting up close and smashing enemies with Fire based attacks. The Ice Dragon being more like a Sniper/Mage class with Ice/slowing attacks to freeze or take them out from a distance. The Acid Dragon being a Necromancer with Acid based attacks causing DOTS and summoning zombies to take the focus off of you.

Now in terms of actually flying and battling, is very awkward. You move around by clicking where you want to fly, and your dragon to fly to the beacon you placed. Then attacking enemies you have to select a spell, and either click or click and hold to power up the spell. Most spells though will cause you to stop before actually attacking, causing you to attack then trying to move to avoid being hit. This tend to make the game feel very awkward for me, and kind of why I never completely finished the game.

I played the game for about 8 hours before I added in the Fan-made patches. I highly recommend adding the patches.

Pros:
- You are a god damn mother f***ing Dragon!
- Lots of good attacks/spells to use, that feel powerful to use.
- Leveling system is simple to use.
- Audio/Music sound great.
- Has a much needed Tutorial.
- Steam Trading Cards.

Cons:
- Very outdated graphics.
- Controls are bad.
- Audio/Video problems.
- Extremely repetitive.
- **Requires Fan-made Patches to make the game better.**
- No achievements.

If you can look past the problems, it can be a good game. Not perfect, but GOOD. When in doubt, get it on sale!

Absolute blast from the past from my childhood. Having a dragon that helps the humans as player character is by itself a daring move, then hiding an indirect strategy game and an action-rpg underneath it is even more. By today's standards the game can be seen as far from perfect, but the things that worked back in the day do still rock, and I dare to say that since The I of the Dragon happened, I have never seen another game like this.

The graphics are simple but timeless enough to not make the game bad today, there is a pretty cool terrain deformation system, some spells let you raise mountains or volcanoes from the ground, and I mean a 100 meter tall wall of earth, you're giant compared to the tiny humans, one badly placed spell might tear down half of the city you just helped build. 

You play as either a magic, necromancy or fighting dragon and have to help save humanity from an evil monster. Period. On your way to victory you level up and unlock interesting new abilities. Building your dragon is straightforward, each of them has certain core skills that take less skill points to level up than others, but that does not exclude you from creating an ability-based fighting dragon or a magic dragon with a strong ice breath. They play very differently due to the 20 or so skills each of them unlocks, and as such I found the game pretty replayable. There also seems to be no level cap, so one can grind their way up. And that's it, you clear out monsters, get stronger, build some cities and win the game. Cities themselves have a linear upgrade path and will start collecting energy, you have to make sure that they don't get torn down by the incoming armies of fairly varied monsters. Every region you will discover a new foe.

The controls are atrocious and I suggest reading some guides on how to add a .dll file that makes your customized control scheme save. The pacing is a bit slow, but the game actually has an option to slow down or accelerate time. There are some parts where you play as another character, those are absolute junk but can't be skipped. The basic gameplay loop still works, most old games I pick up these days lost all their charm, while this game doesn't give a damn about a good story or anything to quality VO, the base design just works so well and I found myself spending an entire weekend replaying the game as a monster-summoning dragon mage that spams armies on his enemies. 

In the age of reboots this would most certainly be a suitable candidate.

When I first found this game (the original NON-STEAM version), I thought that it was gonna be really bad, my first impression of it didn't really convince me, but I started playing it anyway to give it a chance. I found it to be a lot of fun, I very much enjoy the premise of the game (Play as a dragon), I like the music and it feels really good to cast a powerful spell that obliterates everything below you. 

That being said, both the original and the steam version of this game have their issues. Both of them don't play the in-game music, the original was unable to save customized keybindings and running this game in compatibility mode caused major problems for me back when I first tried it. However all of these issues can be resolved by downloading a few fixes, which repair the missing in-game music and the keybindings.

The steam version changed a few things from the old original. The intro movie is a shortened version of the 4 minute original which explained the full backstory of the game. The short version does not really explain it properly. The music is also different, since each regional edition of the original seems to have a different soundtrack so the steam version has it's own soundtrack too.
I also experienced a minor issue with the steam edition only. My loading times in between different menus (world map, level-up menu, main menu etc.) seem to be much longer than in the old original, where they are almost instantaneous. But other than that it's running just fine.


My conclusion is, while I personally prefer the older original version for minor reasons, the steam version is basically the same game with different music and intro video. I really like this game, and if you enjoy dragons, I think you are going to like this game as well once you get used to the dated controls.


(One word of advice: Better stay away from the North american original version of the game published by StrategyFirst, since I've heard that it causes a lot of game crashes for multiple people. Better get the EU version or steam version.)

EDIT: I found out what exactly caused these weird longer loading times in between menus. It's a file in the game directory called "dimap.dll". Deleting this file will make these loading times in between menus near instant again, however it will make you unable to set custom keybindings. Though that is not such a big problem really, since this game plays best with a mouse and just a few keys mostly anyway ;)

EDIT 2: I recommend buying this game on GOG instead, since it already comes with pretty much all of the bugfixes included, while in the steam version you have to fix them yourself. [h1]The Good[/h1]
This game follows extremely rare concept that every true dragon lover will like: you control a dragon, so the dragon is not a "flying horse" for human character, and you don't have to fight against any other dragons.
This is RPG style game where you level up, increase your skills and unlock new magic abilities to be even better. Fighting is quite slow but satisfying. It's projectile-based combat and you are flying 100% of the time. You need to fly around(and up and down) to avoid most of the damage. There are 12 areas and it's always the same rule - there are "lairs" you need to destroy, if there is no human town, they respawn after some time. If you built human town, they don't despawn. Most of time it's about getting human town to X level(by destroying enemies) and destroy lairs. There are some different things to make things varied however like having to destroy super-lair, some different kind of enemies, or the town of humans who teamed up with the enemy. Sometimes it's easy and tiring to get rid of these lairs. Sometime you get into there "oh crap" moments where there are tons of enemies and you can't just force through them.

The story is here to give some meaning. It's extremely simple. Short introduction:
There was a time when dragons helped humans to get rid of the Skarborr - an evil demon. After that there a peace but after some time humans started to make some actions against dragons. Disappointed, they left lands of humans to live away from them but the dragon god, Ungh-Agor, left a prophecy that in 100 years Skarborr will return and only dragon will be able to stop him. Then he left an egg in some temple. There were believers of the dragon god who kept this in their hearts. Finally the Skarborr came and some time after, the dragon from that one egg arrived.
The dragon who hatched from that egg is you.

There are three choices of your character which you need to make immediately when begining new game: 
 - Annoth, the Fire Breather - your specialization will be raw breath power with minimal use of magic.
 - Barroth, the Magician - low HP but great magic skills both for attacks and supporting yourself. Your breath will be used rarely. He has extremely difficult start in the game, so be prepared for it when choosing him.
 - Morrogh, the Necromancer - an extremely versitale character, you can't go wrong with him. High survivability and abilities to summon various creatures to help you.

Personaly I played Morrogh and I enjoyed him. Some of his magic skills are useless and other are great but by the end he was extremely satisfying to play.

Some soundtrack tracks are very nice. Some are played too often and get repetitive but there are few gems around. You can find these in Data>Sounds>Ambience folder in game files.

[h1]The Bad[/h1]
The game has few bugs. Very rarely it can crash when saving. You can choose the language in Steam Properties of the game but be prepared - it will make your existing save in other language useless - they will crash on load. Some things are not explained, like the fact that magic skill recharge is global, so recharging a skill, when different one also recharges is slower than recharging just that skill and nothing more, or the fact that catching skill shows you what you can catch - the point on the arrow becomes bright green.
I also encountered some bug that prevented me to catch creatures to eat.

Controls are weird. What I suggest is to map movement to WSAD, down-up to alt-space, skill casting to Q. Use WSAD to move around and right-mouse-click to cast spells. Moving your character with mouse is bad and the "auto aim skill" works badly. There's one problem however. If you make custom mapping, all dialogs in the game(menu, skill tree) will freeze the game for few seconds. Outside of tutorial it's not that annoying as you may think so you can live with it.. You can "fix" it by deleting "dimap.dll" file in the main game folder but it will also erase your mapping. 

The voice acting... oh. It exists but it's emotionless. At the beginning, when the "old man on the carpet" sees you the first time, his voice is the most emotionless voice someone can have when humanity is close to extinction and the saviour from the prophecy arrives.

Also, humans and the dragon a lot but they don't give much in return. I guess that it wasn't well thought when they made the story, but the story is weak anyway...

There are some missions where you take control of human characters for a moment. All of these missions are bad. These humans characters get killed in two shots. The first time you get a mission like that, the map has enemies with homing projectiles - it's a hell. You need to endure these parts.

Save breaking. Do not keep everything under single save. Sometimes missions can break, for example you need to upgrade the town but you already killed everyone on the map - oops. Or you need to escort supplies to the town but meanwhile the town got destroyed.

If you play Morrogh, some spawned creatures can sit and do nothing during fight. It's because they are mostly immobile and some of them have higher "attention" range than their attack range. It means that they can wait for one enemy out of range to get in their range even while these are 5 other enemies in their range, even next to them and even attacking them.

The UI also doesn't scale with resolution, meaning it will be extremely small on Full HD. It's not that bad however.

And finally when you go in the end, there's a huge fight between human and Skarborr armies. But all you can do is to watch stupid AI fight because you are spawned only after one side loses.

[h1]Conclusions[/h1]
As a dragon lover I liked the game. Yeah it's old but I enjoy old games too. It has bugs but if you want to play a dragon game where you don't need to fight against any dragon, there are very few choices.

The game has a nice amount of detail, the dragon grows and visually changes. Each of the 3 dragons play a bit differently.

I of the Dragon is half RPG and half dragon combat simulator.
Despite the appearance, I of the Dragon isn't a flight simulator, if you were expecting something like Descent: Freespace, Wing Commander, or Tachyon: The Fringe (with dragons instead of spaceships), you will be badly disappointed.

The awesome:
-An original concept - role-playing game with a flying character in an open-world, respawning, nonlinear environment
-Amazing graphics (for its time)
-Build and maintain towns and cities.

The good:
-Dozens of abilities to use and 3 different dragons.
-Build your dragon any way you with attribute points

The bad:
-Various balance and game design problems. Some abilities are overpowered, others are bad, and the in-game descriptions of abilities and attributes aren't descriptive enough. There's no way to roll back or refund attribute points.
-There's no way to rebind the keys, and it looks like there's never going to be an official patch to fix this.

The unacceptable:
-The UI is bad enough to sink the entire game. The camera swings around wildly and there's no way to bind it to mouse movement. UI buttons aren't scaled with resolution, giving you a choice between bad resolution or small buttons. But wait, it gets even worse. The left/right steering randomly stops working (and this happens often). Obviously in any game that requires dodging projectiles, being able to steer or strafe is required, and this problem ruins the game so badly I can't recommend it.

The verdict:
An otherwise great game completely ruined with severe UI/control issues bordering on unplayable. If you're going to buy this, wait for at least an 80% discount - and only if you like role-playing games, flight games, and/or dragons.

This game's combat feels more like a watered-down Baldur's Gate where you only have one party member. In theory, the addition of two extra axes of movement should make movement more involved. In theory, capitalism works.

Ideally, controlling a dragon in flight should make you feel powerful, and your enemies should feel insurmountable to mere mortals. A game where you control a dragon SHOULD feel much faster-paced and more exciting, but this fails to deliver on both fronts.
